1:
Gill places the passage by what precedes it, since after the laws touching the purity of the priests, the perfection of their sacrifices and the feasts the people were to keep, God now speaks of some other things concerning priests and people together; and he notes that Moses, as chief magistrate under God and clothed with authority from him, had power to command what was required. Ellicott makes the same transition in fewer words, that the regulations about the annual festivals and their ritual are now followed by directions for the daily service, and he marks something singular in the wording: this is the only other place in Leviticus where God orders Moses to command rather than to impart or communicate his will, though the command itself occurs almost literally in Exodus. Henry supposes the older law is repeated here because it was now beginning to be put in execution, once other things were settled. On the oil he insists on quality, since the people were to provide it and, like everything else used in God's service, it must be of the best — pure olive oil, beaten, and probably double-strained. From that he takes his own turn: ministers are as burning and shining lights in Christ's church, but it is the duty of the people to provide comfortably for them, as Israel did for the lamps, since scandalous maintenance makes a scandalous ministry.

A small grammatical oddity catches both the puritan voices. Henry observes that the English copies read lamps throughout, whereas the Hebrew has the singular in the second verse and the plural in the fourth, and Wesley repeats the point after him: the seven lamps made all one lamp, in allusion to which the blessed Spirit of grace is represented by seven lamps of fire before the throne, for there are diversities of gifts but one Spirit.

The tending of them is a duty as well as the providing. Henry describes the work — the priests must snuff the lamps, clean the candlestick and supply them with oil morning and evening — and reads it as a figure of the gospel ministry, whose business is to hold forth the word of life, not to set up new lights but by expounding and preaching to make the light of it more clear and extensive. He adds a comfort against the failure of that ministry: this was the ordinary way of keeping the lamps burning, but when the church was poor and in distress we find its lamps fed constantly with oil from the good olives immediately, without the service of priest or people, for though God has tied us to means he has not tied himself to them, and will take effectual care that his lamp never go out in the world for want of oil. Wesley notes only that Aaron did the work either by himself or by his sons. Of the place, Gill explains that without the vail means on the outside of the vail dividing the holy from the holy of holies, before the ark in which the testimony lay, and Ellicott confirms it is the second vail, correcting two phrases besides — better the tent of meeting, and better a statute for ever throughout your generations. Why the candlestick is called pure they answer differently. Gill gives two reasons out of Jarchi, partly that it was made of pure gold and partly that the priest was to keep it pure and clean and free from ashes, and Wesley says the same; Ellicott grants that Exodus suggests the first, but reports that the authorities of the second Temple read the verse as an order of procedure — that Aaron shall arrange the lamps after having purified and cleaned the candlestick and removed all the cinders.
5:
Keil notes that the shewbread and its use are described here for the first time, though it had already been offered at the consecration of the tabernacle and set out by Moses. Gill says only that the flour was of wheat, and the finest of it, and Wesley that the baking fell to the priests or Levites. Ellicott reports the whole process as the second Temple remembered it. Twenty-four seahs of wheat, brought as a meat offering, were beaten and ground and passed through twelve sieves each finer than the last; the dough was kneaded outside the court and shaped in golden moulds, so that each loaf came out ten handbreadths long, five broad, one finger thick and square at each end. Each was made of two omers, the quantity appointed to supply one person for a day, so that he takes every loaf to stand for the food of a man and his neighbour while the twelve answer to the tribes — a reading the ancient Chaldee makes explicit. Calvin says the same, that it can hardly be doubted they were twelve with reference to the tribes, as if God would admit to his board the food offered by each.

How they lay on the table is disputed. Wesley says flatly that the two rows were not one loaf above another but one beside another, arguing it from the incense set upon each; Ellicott would render the word piles rather than rows and describes them as placed one upon another in two stacks, laid lengthwise across the board, so that being ten handbreadths long they overhung its six-handbreadth width at either side. He adds that the second-Temple authorities took upon the pure table strictly, the loaves resting on the board itself and not upon the hollow golden rods set between them to let air pass and keep them from going mouldy through the week. The frankincense he would likewise set by each stack rather than upon it, the two bowls standing in the handbreadths of board left spare — in the later practice, in a gap between them. Gill, following Jarchi, describes two cups with a handful in each. Calvin is content with what the incense was for: he refers the memorial to it rather than to the bread, as if the loaves, seasoned by the smell of it, renewed the memory of the children of Israel so that they should be of sweet savour before God.

The weekly change Gill and Ellicott describe alike, both drawing on one rabbinic account: four priests went in carrying the new bread and the incense, four having gone before them to lift away the old; the one party stood on the north with faces southward and the other on the south with faces northward, and as the old was raised the new was set down, their hands exactly over against each other, because it is written before me continually. Wesley draws doctrine out of that detail, the covenant being called everlasting not only because it was to last as long as the Jewish polity but because the thing itself was continual. Ellicott adds that they were bought with the people's half-shekels. What became of the old bread is agreed. Gill says the loaves were divided between the courses that carried in and brought out, the high priest taking half from each; Ellicott gives the division as six for the high priest and six among the officiating priests, and observes that of all the perquisites falling to them only eight had to be eaten inside the sanctuary, this being one. Calvin puts the whole institution in a sentence: this was no ordinary symbol of God's favour, since the loaves were called the bread of faces because set before his eyes, who by them made known his special kindness, descending familiarly to his people as if he came to banquet with them.
10:
Evil manners, says Henry, beget good laws. Neither the offender nor his father is named, only his mother, who was an Israelite, and Henry takes the notice of it two ways: it may hint at the occasion of the quarrel, or it may show the common ill effect of mixed marriages — when a daughter of Israel would marry an idolatrous Egyptian, what could be the fruit of such a match but a blasphemer? for children are apt to take after the worse side, and will sooner learn of an Egyptian father to blaspheme than of an Israelitish mother to pray. Wesley makes the same use of it, adding that such severity against a man who was a stranger by his father and an Israelite by his mother shows God would not have this sin go unpunished among his people, whoever committed it. Ellicott supplies the woman's name, Shelomith, and notes that since the father never appears he evidently stayed behind in Egypt. Calvin sees providence in that very fact: it was ordered that the first example of this severity should fall on the son of an Egyptian, for if God so harshly avenged the insult of his name upon the offspring of a foreigner, impiety was far less excusable in Israelites.

What the quarrel was about the text does not say, and the commentators fill it in from the same tradition. Ellicott reports that the man of Israel was a Danite, and that this half-Egyptian contended he had a right from his mother's side to encamp among the children of Dan, while the Danite maintained that a son might pitch only by the standard of his father's house. Henry adds the moral: the mixed multitude were often the authors of strife, and the way to preserve the peace of the church is to preserve the purity of it. When quarrels begin we know not what mischief they will make before they end, and when men's passion is up they forget both their reason and their religion. Ellicott corrects the phrase describing his coming, since he went out into the midst of the children of Israel, which shows he lived outside the camp and came where he had no right to be; Calvin takes it to mean in public, since had the crime been secret he could never have been convicted by witnesses. Calvin refuses the excuse the quarrel offers: though the blasphemy escaped him in anger, punishment followed all the same, since nothing is more intolerable than that our wrath should vent itself upon God because we are angry with a fellow-creature.

What name he blasphemed is the chapter's crux, and Clarke argues at length that it was not the name we assume. The text does not say Jehovah; it says he pierced, or distinguished, or expressed the name — and though the later Jews, holding it impious to pronounce the sacred name, put hashshem in its place, that word was never so used before rabbinical superstition. Houbigant therefore supposed the man had sworn by one of his own country's gods, and Clarke thinks hashshem may well be the name of an Egyptian deity — a reading countenanced by the distinction drawn later between the man who curses his god and the man who blasphemes the name of the Lord. Henry assumes the plainer sense, that he blasphemed God, who is known by his name only; but he rejects as a fond conceit the notion of the superstitious Jews that the offence lay in pronouncing the name of Jehovah, since he who made himself known by that name never forbade men to call him by it. Calvin takes the same verb a third way, not as expressing but as transfixing, and thinks the metaphor apt, God's name being pierced through when it is insultingly abused. Gill notes only that his name and his mother's are given a little later.
11:
Gill reports the Jewish understanding and then declines it. By the name blasphemed the Jews generally mean Jehovah, which they hold ineffable and say ought not to be pronounced except by the high priest in the sanctuary, whereas this man expressed it in its proper sound and used it to curse the man who strove with him — the Mishnah ruling that a blasphemer is not guilty until he expresses the name. But it undoubtedly means, Gill says, blaspheming God himself, by whatsoever name. Ellicott explains how the text came to read as it does: the word Name was substituted for the Tetragrammaton by a copyist who out of reverence would not set cursing beside it, the same shyness having introduced Lord and God for Jehovah in sundry other places; and he notes that during the second Temple the clause was read he pronounced the Name and cursed. Wesley takes the omission the other way, as an aggravation rather than a reverence — the words of the Lord are supplied here from a later verse, and their absence lets the offence fall on the Name simply, so called by way of eminency, that name which is above every name and which a man should in some sort tremble to mention.

Why he was kept in prison the voices agree upon, and the reason is a gap in the law. Ellicott observes that confinement as a punishment is nowhere enacted in the Mosaic legislation, so the ward was custody and not sentence: though cursing an earthly parent was already capital, no law had fixed the punishment for cursing the heavenly Father, nor was it known whether such an offender should be left to God himself to deal with. Wesley says the same shortly: God had declared he would not hold such guiltless, but not how he would have them punished by men. Gill adds only that the prison was a known place in the camp, as Aben Ezra observes. Ellicott and Gill both suppose the answer came from the sanctuary, where God had promised to commune with Moses from the mercy-seat, though Ellicott is careful that the text nowhere says how the appeal was made. Calvin fastens on the same point: this punishment was not inflicted by man's caprice or the headstrong zeal of the people, but Moses was instructed by divine revelation what sentence to pronounce.

The sentence sends him outside. Gill takes the place to be significant as well as customary, since it showed he had no part nor lot in Israel and was unworthy of their church state, though the place of stoning was in any case without the camp; Ellicott adds that this was where unclean persons had to abide and where malefactors were executed. What the laying on of hands meant is read two ways. Keil makes it a transfer: by resting their hands on the blasphemer's head the hearers were to throw off from themselves the blasphemy they had heard and return it upon his head for him to expiate. Clarke and Ellicott make it testimony instead. Clarke says it was by this ceremony that those who heard him curse bore their public witness, without which his punishment would not have been lawful, and that by it they said in effect, Thy blood be upon thy own head; Ellicott specifies that both the witnesses who heard and the judges who condemned laid on their hands, that the rite was peculiar to a blasphemer under sentence of death, and that by it they declared testimony and sentence alike to be faithful and righteous, saying, Let thy blood be upon thine own head. Calvin's phrase falls between the two, that they laid their hands on him as if to throw the whole blame upon him. Ellicott closes the procedure: the witnesses, as representatives of the people, cast the first stone.
15:
Whose god is meant by the first clause divides the readings sharply. Ellicott takes it of the heathen's own: since the criminal who occasioned the law was an Egyptian, directions are given first about Gentiles sojourning among the Hebrews who have not renounced faith in their own deity, so that if such a man curses the god he still professes to believe in, he shall bear his sin, suffering at the hands of his own co-religionists, while the Israelites are not to interfere to save him, since a heathen who reviles the god he believes in is not to be trusted in anything else. The others take the clause of the true God. Clarke reads curseth as makes light of, of one who does not treat God and sacred things with due reverence; Wesley says the same shortly, that to curse is to speak of God reproachfully and to bear one's sin is to bear the punishment of it. Calvin makes the verse the guard of the third commandment, whose object was that God's holy name should be honoured with the veneration it deserves, seeing that the insult which violates it is here made capital; and by cursing he understands all profane words that brand it with dishonour — whether a man accuse God of injustice or designedly detract from his glory, since many when exasperated launch out into blasphemies while others parade their audacity by scoffing at him.

The verb of the second clause comes up again. Gill records that from the wording the Jews gather that the name Jehovah must be expressed or there is no blasphemy, and answers that the offence is not the bare using of the word but speaking ill and contemptuously of God with respect to any of his names or any of his perfections, ways and works. Clarke gives the range of the verb, that it means to pierce or transfix, though some render it to expound. Calvin canvasses the same word and decides against one option: it means to hollow out or perforate, and by metaphor to unfold, but the rendering he who shall have expressed is lame, and transfix seems to him the suitable word. On the manner of death he sees two purposes: the offender is stoned by the whole people, that all may learn such a monster should be annihilated as contaminating the earth, and that God may prove the zeal of his people. Wesley reads it the same way, that the congregation acted to show their zeal and to beget in themselves a greater dread of the crime.

That the law binds the stranger as well as the native is the point of what follows. Calvin observes that God subjected to this punishment not only the Jews but the strangers dwelling among them in the way of business, and did so precisely that the crime might be punished the more severely in his own servants, who were less excusable. Ellicott makes the same connection for what follows, since the enactments about murder and personal injury had been given before and are repeated to show that, like blasphemy, they apply to Gentile and Jew alike;. Wesley finds a nearer reason, that the law is repeated to prevent the mischief of men's striving together, which here produced blasphemy and elsewhere might lead to murder. Clarke sets the two crimes side by side: he who blasphemes God is a curse in society, and he who wilfully takes away the life of any man should certainly be put to death, God having absolutely required that life shall go for life. Of the beast Calvin draws a wider principle, that a man must make satisfaction for a loss even where he turned none of it to his own profit — whoever will not care for a neighbour's advantage as much as his own being accounted guilty of theft before God.
19:
The law of like for like is defended by Calvin and qualified by Gill. Calvin thinks it necessary, since without it any accomplished villain might break his brother's leg and then laugh not only at the poor man but at God and his Law; and he answers two objections. It is no injustice, because God does not command an eye for an eye until he has laid down that the rule holds only where a man has knowingly and wilfully inflicted the injury, so that accidental blows are not brought to justice but a premeditated crime only. It is also why the distinction between beast and man is drawn where it is: the loss of an animal may be repaid, whereas if a man is killed no money can make just compensation. Gill will not have the words taken strictly at all, understanding by breach for breach and eye for eye the price or value of them, to be rendered in a pecuniary way.

How far one law for all extends is read three ways. Ellicott confines it to the cases just adduced rather than to blasphemy, which had been dealt with already, so that the same penal statutes bind non-Israelite and stranger in these matters. Wesley limits it differently, to matters of common right and not to church privileges. Calvin opens it widest of all: lest the people of Israel should suppose with their usual arrogance that the race of Abraham alone was privileged, the law is extended to foreigners, and God shows the whole body of the human race to be under his care, so that he would not have even those farthest off exposed to the licentious violence of the ungodly — for though in other points he provided special privileges for his elect people, here, because he created all men without exception after his own image, he takes them under his protection that none might injure them with impunity. Clarke turns the verse into a political maxim. Equal laws, where each individual receives the same protection and the same privileges, are the boast only of a sound constitution; he who obeys the laws has a right to protection, and his person and property are as sacred in the sight of justice as the prince's, while he who does not obey forfeits all title to it.

The sentence is then carried out. Keil records it in a line, that after these laws had been issued the punishment was inflicted, and Gill that the people led him out of the camp, laid their hands upon him and stoned him until he died. Clarke is anxious that the manner of it should not be mistaken for a lynching: we are not to suppose the culprit was exposed to the unbridled fury of the thousands of Israel, which would be brutality and not justice. He gives the Jewish account of the procedure instead — the condemned man brought outside the camp because his crime had made him unclean, stripped within four cubits of the place of execution, the witnesses going up with him to lay their hands on him, and then one of them striking him with a stone upon the loins, after which, if he still lived, they took up a stone as great as two men could lift and threw it upon his breast. Where a man was stoned by a mob, Clarke adds, brutal rage armed every man, justice was set aside, and the will and fury of the people were law, judge, jury and executioner at once. Wesley ends the chapter on a comparison: this blasphemer was the first that died by the law of Moses, as Stephen was the first that died for the gospel and died by the abuse of that same law — the martyr and the malefactor suffering the same death, and yet how vast the difference between them.
